items.q: What is a 'tracer bullet' in this build method?
options: A test that checks every feature at once
The fastest-running version of the app
One thin slice that goes end-to-end through every layer, built before anything wide

explain.right: A tracer bullet is a skinny path through all layers (e.g. button → stored → shown) to prove the whole thing connects early.
explain.wrong: It's not about speed, polish, or testing everything — it's the thinnest complete path, built first.

items.q: Why build a thin end-to-end slice before building the app 'wide'?
options: Building wide first is always faster
It proves the whole path connects and surfaces risky unknowns while the app is still tiny and easy to change
It looks more impressive to show off
So the user interface is pretty before anything works

explain.right: Going thin-but-complete de-risks the connections early, while fixes are cheap — the opposite of a pretty front end wired to nothing.
explain.wrong: 'Wide first' and 'UI first' are the classic beginner traps; the goal is de-risking, not appearance.

items.q: What's the best way to let the AI build your app?
options: Never look at the code since you can't read it anyway
Let it run unattended and check back in an hour
Accept one giant code dump and hope it works
Ask for one small change at a time and review each before the next

explain.right: Small, reviewed steps keep the blast radius small — if something breaks you know which change did it.
explain.wrong: Big dumps and unattended runs leave you unable to review or locate problems; you stay the driver.

items.q: Why commit (save a snapshot) after each working step?
options: It deploys the app to the internet
You always have a recent known-good point to roll back to if the next change breaks something
It's the only way to run the code
It makes the app run faster

explain.right: Frequent commits are checkpoints: when a later change breaks things, you return to the last good snapshot.
explain.wrong: Committing doesn't affect speed, deploy, or whether code runs — it's your safety net of save points.

items.q: Why isn't a feature 'done' just because the AI wrote it and the code looks right?
rubric: Reading code is a guess; you must actually run/execute it
You observe the real behavior (screen, terminal, logs)
You verify it against the spec / acceptance criteria

explain.right: Good answers say you only know it works by running it and watching it behave, then checking it against the spec.
explain.wrong: A weak answer trusts that code which 'looks right' is correct — running it is what proves it.
